scenario: WIBTA if I told my cousin his kid can’t stay in our house? | My cousin (M27) recently moved in with my husband and I. We completely closed of the very large main bedroom and bathroom to create a flatlet for him that’s separate from the house with his own entrance so it’s basically two separate units of one house. Now my cousin has a 2 year old and he’s busy with a custody battle with his ex so he can get to spend more time with his son. I completely support this and really hopes he gets more time with his son. Yesterday my cousin came to ask me if it would be possible for my husband and I to convert our spare bedroom into a room for his son if and when he comes to visit over weekends. There is no access from my cousin’s room into our part of the house and he doesn’t have keys to come and go as he pleases. I understand that the court will be looking into his living situation to see if he has suitable space for his son to stay with him (and to be honest his current room and bathroom is more than big enough) but I’m not comfortable with letting his son sleep in our house if my cousin has no access to him and I’m not willing to take responsibility for his kid. The whole family is involved in this because that’s just the way my family is and everyone expects me to help out my cousin with his current custody situation to get him more time with his son. WIBTA for telling him I will not allow his son to sleep in our house and completely jeopardizing his court case?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's right or wrong for me to tell my cousin that his kid can't stay in our house. Let me break this down step by step. First, my cousin moved in with my husband and me. We converted the main bedroom and bathroom into a separate flatlet for him, so he has his own entrance. That means our living spaces are completely separate. He has a 2-year-old, and he's going through a custody battle with his ex. I support him because I want him to spend more time with his son. Yesterday, he asked if we could convert our spare bedroom into a room for his son when he comes over weekends. But here's the thing: there's no access from his room into our part of the house, and he doesn't have keys to come and go as he pleases. I understand that the court is looking into his living situation to see if he has suitable space for his son. Honestly, his current room and bathroom are more than big enough. But I'm not comfortable letting his son sleep in our house because my cousin doesn't have access to him, and I don't want to take responsibility for his kid. The whole family is involved because that's just how my family is. Everyone expects me to help out my cousin with his custody situation to get him more time with his son. So, if I tell him I won't allow his son to stay in our house, would that be wrong? It could jeopardize his court case. Hmm, so I need to consider a few things here. First, my comfort level and boundaries. I don't feel comfortable having his son in our house because I don't have control over when he comes or goes. That's a valid concern. I don't want to be responsible for his child, especially if I'm not prepared for it. On the other hand, my cousin is going through a tough time, and the family expects me to help. But I also have to think about my own home and the rules I set. If I say no, am I being selfish, or am I respecting my own boundaries? I also need to think about the legal aspect. The court is evaluating his living situation. If he can't have his son stay with him because of our decision, that might affect his custody case negatively. But is that our responsibility? Or is it up to him to provide a suitable environment? I guess another angle is communication. Maybe instead of outright saying no, I could discuss alternative solutions with him. Perhaps there's a way to make the spare bedroom accessible without compromising our privacy. Or maybe he can find another arrangement for his son's stays. But if I'm not comfortable, then maybe it's better to set that boundary. It's important to respect my own limits, even if it's hard for the family. I don't want to end up in a situation where I'm stressed or uncomfortable because of this. So, weighing all these factors, I think it's more about respecting my boundaries and ensuring that my home remains a safe and comfortable space for me and my husband. While supporting my cousin is important, I also need to take care of my own well-being.
